speaker: Jeff Currie
title: Jeff Currie on the 'Volatility Trap' Keeping Commodity Prices So High
question: In global energy markets, why is importing liquefied natural gas a poor long-term foundation for heavy manufacturing economies?
guest: I want to emphasize the following, and I've talked to many German industrialists who made this point: the German industrial manufacturing base can't operate off of LNG. Move the BMW plant to the US and build the BMWs on top of the gas plant and then export the BMWs, or build the BMWs in Qatar. Move the gas to heat people, but you can't run an industrial base off of liquefied gas. I've never been a fan of that. Think about what this thing is: a $300 million floating thermos that is frozen, and you pump a bunch of gas into it and move it around the world. It's a lot easier to move manufactured goods on bulk shipped containers than it is in LNG tankers. So I'm not a fan of using it to run a manufacturing economy, though it does work for heating and things like that. Is it the most viable solution thinking about it on a longer-term basis? It's probably not.

points.core: Liquefying natural gas for cryogenic tanker transport imposes prohibitive structural energy costs.
points.note: Accept: freezing gas and shipping it in specialized multi-hundred-million-dollar LNG tankers is far costlier than pipeline gas. Do not credit: generic claims that energy is expensive or geopolitically risky.

points.core: Shipping finished manufactured goods in containers costs far less than shipping frozen gas.
points.note: Accept: relocating factories to cheap-gas regions and exporting finished products beats transporting LNG to factories. Do not credit: vague mentions of supply-chain localization without the transport-cost comparison.

points.core: Imported liquefied gas remains practical for residential heating rather than competitive industrial production.
points.note: Accept: LNG is viable for heating demand or non-tradable uses but cannot sustain cost-competitive manufacturing bases. Do not credit: blanket claims that LNG has no use at all.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Imported LNG is a structurally expensive and volatile fuel, which is a problem for industries where energy is a large share of costs.

Liquefaction, shipping and regasification typically add several dollars per MMBtu to the price of the gas itself. An LNG-dependent manufacturer therefore always pays well above competitors in places with domestic or pipeline gas, such as the US or the Gulf states. That gap is permanent, and it matters most in energy-intensive sectors like chemicals, fertilizer, steel, glass and aluminum.

Importers are also exposed to a global spot market where cargoes go to the highest bidder. In 2022, European prices rose roughly tenfold, and poorer buyers like Pakistan and Bangladesh were priced out entirely, causing blackouts and factory shutdowns. Long-term contracts reduce this risk but lock in decades-long commitments, often indexed to oil.

Supply also depends on maritime chokepoints such as the Strait of Hormuz, on currency strength and on exporters' politics.

Japan, South Korea and Taiwan do show that LNG-importing industrial economies can thrive. They do it by specializing in high-value manufacturing, where energy is a smaller share of costs.

points.why: The response identifies liquefaction, transport, and regasification as structural costs that put LNG-dependent manufacturers at a disadvantage against competitors using domestic or pipeline gas.

An LNG-dependent manufacturer therefore always pays well above competitors in places with domestic or pipeline gas

points.why: The response omits the cost comparison between shipping finished goods and shipping LNG.
The response explains the cost disadvantage for energy-intensive manufacturing but never identifies heating or another non-tradable use as a practical application for imported LNG.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
Importing liquefied natural gas locks heavy manufacturing into a permanent structural cost disadvantage. Cooling gas to –162°C, shipping it across oceans in specialized cryogenic tankers, and regasifying it at import terminals adds substantial capital and energy overhead—often doubling or tripling landed prices compared to domestic pipeline gas in producer regions like the United States or the Middle East. Because industries such as chemicals, fertilizers, steel, and glass consume vast, continuous volumes of gas as both high-temperature fuel and chemical feedstock, structurally higher input prices erode thin operating margins and drive industrial offshoring.

Beyond baseline cost, seaborne LNG exposes manufacturers to severe price volatility and geopolitical vulnerability. Spot cargoes flow to the highest global bidder, meaning weather shocks, terminal outages, or maritime chokepoint disruptions anywhere in the world rapidly spike domestic industrial energy bills, undermining the multi-decade cost predictability that capital-intensive plants require. Finally, energy-intensive liquefaction and shipping inflate LNG’s lifecycle carbon and methane footprint, leaving import-reliant industries increasingly exposed to escalating carbon pricing, border adjustments, and stranded-asset risks as global competitors electrify.

points.why: The response explicitly ties liquefaction and cryogenic shipping to a structural cost premium over pipeline gas.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer: Importing LNG is a structurally expensive and volatile base for energy-hungry industry like steel, chemicals, fertilizer, glass and aluminum. Liquefying gas, shipping it and regasifying it adds roughly $3–6 per MMBtu over pipeline or domestic gas. That leaves importers paying well above US Henry Hub prices even in calm markets. LNG is also priced against a global market, so importers compete with every other buyer for spare cargoes. Europe's 2022 crisis showed what that means: Asian and European spot prices briefly passed $70/MMBtu, and ammonia and aluminum plants shut, some for good. Manufacturers that compete against US producers or Gulf state plants with cheap local feedstock can't absorb that gap for long. Importers also face supply risk from chokepoints like Hormuz, dependence on a few exporting countries, and long take-or-pay contracts that lock in fossil fuel costs as carbon prices rise and electrified or hydrogen-based processes improve. That said, it isn't fatal. Japan, South Korea and Taiwan built major industrial economies on imported LNG by using long-term contracts, efficiency and higher-value products. LNG works better as a bridge or backup than as the main cost advantage.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer:
Relying on imported liquefied natural gas puts heavy manufacturing economies at a permanent structural disadvantage. Because LNG requires capital-intensive liquefaction, specialized cryogenic shipping, and regasification, its landed cost is inherently higher than the domestic or pipeline gas available to competitors in producer nations like the United States or the Middle East. For energy-intensive industries such as steel, chemicals, glass, and fertilizers—which sell commoditized goods on thin margins—this persistent energy premium steadily erodes global competitiveness.

Beyond high baseline costs, LNG exposes manufacturers to severe price volatility and geopolitical risk. Because seaborne cargoes move to the highest bidder, a supply disruption or cold winter in one region can abruptly spike prices worldwide, undermining the predictable economics required for multi-decade factory investments. Dependence on maritime chokepoints and dollar-denominated imports adds further strategic and currency vulnerability. Finally, as carbon pricing and border adjustments expand globally, anchoring heavy industry to imported fossil gas risks locking economies into high-emissions assets that become increasingly uncompetitive over time.

points.why: The response directly attributes LNG’s persistent cost premium to liquefaction, cryogenic shipping, and regasification.

Imported liquefied natural gas (LNG) is a weak long-term foundation for heavy manufacturing because it makes a major input cost depend on global fuel markets. Liquefaction, shipping, and regasification add costs, which can put manufacturers at a disadvantage against competitors with access to cheap domestic gas. Importers are also exposed to supply disruptions, competition for cargoes, and exchange-rate swings. Where gas-fired plants set wholesale electricity prices, those shocks can raise power bills across industry.

Steel, chemicals, and fertilizer plants make investments that need to pay off over decades. Long-term LNG contracts can reduce exposure to spot prices, but they may still link prices to oil or gas benchmarks and require buyers to pay for volumes they no longer need. LNG can diversify supply and cover shortages, but relying on it for everyday industrial demand leaves manufacturers exposed to costs they have little control over.

Imported liquefied natural gas (LNG) can fill supply gaps, but it is a costly and volatile foundation for industries that need affordable energy for decades. Liquefying, shipping and regasifying the fuel adds costs that competitors with abundant domestic gas or low-cost electricity can often avoid. When global supplies tighten, importers buying on the spot market must bid against buyers elsewhere. The resulting price spikes can squeeze factories twice, through the gas they use as fuel or feedstock and through electricity prices where gas-fired plants set the price of power.

Heavy manufacturers often sell at world prices, so they have limited room to pass those costs on. Long-term LNG contracts can reduce exposure to price spikes, but they can also lock buyers into purchase commitments even as cleaner technologies become cheaper or carbon costs rise. That combination makes it harder to justify investment in plants expected to operate for decades.
